transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-11
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~43 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood CSM), Aisha Khan (Vectra), Tom Reed (Vectra), Priya Nair (Vectra)

Summary:
Quick sync on TTFT and streaming results from last week's pilot run, review of anomalous p99 spikes, discussion about kernel choices for longer sequence lengths and customer infra constraints (VPC + on-prem gateway), and agreement on next steps to run a larger streaming TTFT benchmark and a kernel deep dive.

Topics: TTFT trends, streaming vs batched tradeoffs, sequence length sensitivity, kernel selection (fused attention / flash / custom kernel), KV cache hit profiles, autoscaling behavior, fallbacks for dedicated vs hosted.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Quick roll call, and then Jordan will run through the perf slides.
[00:19] Aisha Khan: Hey Maya, hi Jordan, Tom here as well. Sorry for a bit late, had a quick deploy.
[00:27] Tom Reed: Yeah, on my side infra is green, the staging cluster is ready for the next run.
[00:33] Jordan Patel: Cool. So to frame the meeting, we got the TTFT traces from last Friday's run — small-scale 2k requests — and a couple of weird p99 jumps around the 60s and 300s token windows. I'll share the slide, but main point is that streaming path improved average TTFT by ~18% but p99 remained sticky.
[00:52] Priya Nair: When you say streaming path, is that the continuous streaming runtime you added or just chunked responses?
[01:02] Jordan Patel: It's the streaming runtime with early prefix flushes — continuous streaming plus prefix KV caching. On our side we call it the stream-kernel path, it's slightly different codegen/dispatch than the batch-only path.
[01:15] Aisha Khan: We saw some tokens early coming back quicker, but then some requests hung at the end, so user perceived latency is still variable.
[01:24] Jordan Patel: Exactly. The variability correlates with sequence length switching mid-request — when clients escalate from short prompts to appended context we see cache invalidation in a couple of cases.
[01:37] Tom Reed: That's the part I worry about — our gateway occasionally strips keep-alive headers and that may cause new connections, which in turn causes cold cache on the backend.
[01:47] Maya Chen: Good callout. We should instrument connection churn separately. Jordan, do you have the KV cache hit-rate numbers?
[01:56] Jordan Patel: Yes — overall hit-rate was ~62% on the short prompt cohort, but it fell to ~18% when sequence length >256 due to our current sharding policy. Also, some of the model variants we bumped had non-ideal key encoding that reduced hit locality.
[02:12] Aisha Khan: Hmm we have a mix of conversational short turns and expanded context explorations — about 30% of requests end up >512 tokens once the user opens a document.
[02:22] Jordan Patel: So two levers: change sharding to use a sequence-aware affinity, or adjust chunking to flatten sequence transitions. There's a cost tradeoff — affinity helps hits but increases lock contention for hot keys on dedicated GPU.
[02:34] Maya Chen: Let's also not forget kernel selection — for seq len 1024 we saw the flash-attention fused kernels outperform baseline GEMM but only on Ampere+ cards. On older T4-like hardware the fallback kernel was slower and spiky.
[02:49] Tom Reed: We're on mixed fleet — some prod-like nodes are Ampere, but our staging has older cards to mirror a customer region. Could we force a kernel selection per-node?
[02:59] Jordan Patel: Yes you can pin kernels per device type; Redwood runtime supports kernel overrides at the pool level. For the pilot we used auto-select which did a poor job when seq distribution changed.
[03:11] Priya Nair: Is that something that would require redeploy?
[03:15] Jordan Patel: No, just a runtime flag and a config update; we can roll it without interrupting in-flight requests if done as a canary.
[03:23] Maya Chen: Luis, quick note — can you remind them about the canary policy?
[03:27] Luis Ortega: Sure, we typically do a 10% pool canary for 30 minutes and watch TTFT and p99. If stable we ramp to 50% then to 100%. We also have an automatic fallback to the previous kernel build if error rate increases by >0.5%.
[03:43] Aisha Khan: That fallback is reassuring. For the p99 spikes we also noticed increased CUDA context switches in the logs at the same times. Could that be from preemption?
[03:54] Jordan Patel: Possibly. The spikes line up with large batched requests hitting the same device and preempting streaming micro-requests. Our recommendation is to split pools by workload type (streaming vs batch) or use fractional vGPU scheduling on Dedicated.
[04:10] Tom Reed: Fractional vGPU scheduling is something ops will need to approve, but splitting pools seems doable. Any quick numbers on cost delta?
[04:18] Maya Chen: We'll include a rough cost delta in the follow-up — Dedicated pool with fractional yields higher utilization but slightly higher management cost. For hosted, the runtime auto-routes to cheaper pool variants but you lose strict isolation.
[04:31] Aisha Khan: Security is another constraint — we need VPC peering and customer-managed KMS. Is that supported in the POC flow?
[04:40] Maya Chen: Yes, for Private we support VPC and KMS/HSM integrations. For the current Hosted pilot we used encrypted at rest with Redwood-managed KMS; we can provide the SOC2 excerpt and a Private deployment quote if you want.
[04:52] Tom Reed: Please send those docs.
[04:54] Maya Chen: Will do — action item for me.
[04:58] Jordan Patel: Back to kernels — we tried 3 kernel families: fused-flash, windowed-attn, and baseline matmul. On seq=64 fused-flash was best; at 1024 windowed-attn reduced peak memory but increased per-token overhead causing worse TTFT for small prefixes.
[05:18] Priya Nair: So there's no single winner across our mixed workload.
[05:22] Jordan Patel: Unfortunately not. The runtime supports model-variant routing: short-request traffic -> fused-flash optimized model variant, long-request traffic -> windowed-attn variant. That buys latency for the majority while protecting for long sequences.
[05:35] Aisha Khan: Can variants be served from same pool? Concerned about memory duplication if both variants resident.
[05:42] Jordan Patel: We prefer separate pools; otherwise memory duplication is real. However, if you have large capacity nodes we can co-locate with memory multiplexing — but that requires specific kernel and quantization compatibility.
[05:54] Tom Reed: Memory multiplexing sounds risky for our compliance. Maybe separate pools is easier to explain to auditors.
[06:01] Maya Chen: Good note. On the streaming TTFT tests you ran, Aisha, what was the client concurrency pattern?
[06:08] Aisha Khan: We used a stepped ramp: 10, 50, 200 concurrent streams over 20 minutes, holding each for 5 minutes. We saw TTFT median stable but p99 jumped when concurrency hit 200.
[06:20] Jordan Patel: That's classic contending for single-device throughput — the runtime's continuous batching tries to aggregate tokens but if streams want low latency we limit batching which reduces device efficiency. Tradeoff.
[06:31] Maya Chen: Any anomalies in tokenization? Sometimes tokenization mismatch across client libraries causes larger effective sequence lengths.
[06:38] Aisha Khan: We used their tokenizer v1.2; there might be tokenization differences vs Redwood's tokenizer v1.3 that causes a 10-12% token count delta in a few templates.
[06:48] Jordan Patel: If you can pin the tokenizer we can normalize. We also have a tokenizer shim we can push into your staging to match counts.
[06:56] Priya Nair: That would be helpful. Also let's note rollout cadence — we have a demo next Tues and product would like a clear note on perceived latency improvements.
[07:05] Maya Chen: We'll aim to have the larger TTFT run done before then.
[07:09] Jordan Patel: One more experiment suggestion: increase KV cache chunk size for long docs so that expansion retains locality. It will increase memory use but might improve hit rates for the >512 cohort.
[07:21] Tom Reed: Memory is constrained on staging, but we can try a single node change to validate.
[07:26] Aisha Khan: We'll do a single-node change first.
[07:29] Jordan Patel: I'll add guidance on chunk sizing and expected memory overhead.
[07:33] Maya Chen: Switching gears: we saw a couple of p99 regressed on one kernel build that had a custom aten fused op; we should pin to the previous build while you validate.
[07:43] Jordan Patel: We already flagged the build and added a fallback to previous build in the canary policy. The telemetry shows an error bump at 2026-02-06 03:10 UTC when the build rolled.
[07:53] Aisha Khan: That lines up with our user reports. Can we get the exact commit and the change log?
[07:58] Jordan Patel: Yes, I'll paste the commit SHA and short changelist in the slack thread after the call.
[08:04] Priya Nair: Regarding metrics - can you produce a single sheet with median, p95, p99, and TTFT for streaming and batch across the 3 kernel families? That would help prioritization.
[08:15] Jordan Patel: Absolutely. I'll produce histograms and a pivot with seq len buckets 64/256/512/1024.
[08:23] Maya Chen: And include cost per 1M tokens estimate for each config.
[08:28] Jordan Patel: Will do.
[08:30] Aisha Khan: For the larger run, what should we instrument at the client side? We can push extra logs.
[08:36] Jordan Patel: We need per-request connection ID, token counts pre/post, prefix hit boolean, and kernel selected. Also, include client-side timing (time to first byte observed) so we can compare.
[08:47] Tom Reed: We'll add those columns.
[08:49] Maya Chen: Luis, can you confirm the SLA implications if we move to Dedicated vs Hosted for this workload?
[08:56] Luis Ortega: Dedicated gives you stricter latency SLOs and more predictable p99 targets because of fixed capacity. Hosted is multitenant and cheaper, but we rely on routing policies to meet latency. For your workload with mixed seq lengths, Dedicated is recommended if strict p99 is a business requirement.
[09:12] Aisha Khan: Business requirement is p99 < 1.2s for short-turn chats. Right now we're at ~1.0 median and p99 around 1.8 in peak.
[09:22] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll tailor the next run to optimize short-turn 64/128 token paths.
[09:28] Jordan Patel: One more note on quantization — 4-bit quant improved memory and throughput slightly but introduced a small accuracy drift in one of your QA prompts. We should run a qualitative eval on the quantized variant before full rollout.
[09:42] Priya Nair: Product will own the eval. We'll compile a small prompt set.
[09:46] Aisha Khan: We'll also validate hallucination rates pre/post quant.
[09:50] Jordan Patel: Back to kernel deep-dive timing; we recommended a dedicated 60m session with Tom and infra — propose 2026-02-24 or 2026-02-25.
[09:59] Tom Reed: The 24th works for me.
[10:02] Maya Chen: I'll propose 24th and add to calendar.
[10:05] Luis Ortega: Quick question from a runbook perspective — if we split pools, how do we route traffic while preserving session affinity for a given user?
[10:14] Jordan Patel: We use session tags on requests; the router honors affinity keys and will keep a user pinned to the same pool for the session TTL. If we need to migrate we do a graceful drain.
[10:25] Aisha Khan: Sounds good. One last item — Tom saw occasional 403s in the logs when the token was rotated on the KMS during a rekey. Is that expected?
[10:34] Maya Chen: Rekeys should be seamless but in some older client libs we saw a 403 during the short window. We'll double-check the KMS integration path and share mitigations.
[10:44] Jordan Patel: I'll attach the KMS retry guidance.
[10:47] Maya Chen: Okay folks, let's recap next steps. Jordan, you'll produce the kernel perf pivot and histograms, and the per-device histograms. Aisha/Tom will run the larger streaming TTFT with the client instrumentation. I'll send the SOC2 excerpt and Dedicated pricing delta. We'll reconvene after the larger run and do the kernel deep-dive on the 24th.
[11:10] Aisha Khan: Thanks everyone.
[11:13] Tom Reed: Thanks.
[11:15] Priya Nair: Appreciate it.
[11:18] Maya Chen: End of call.
